name: Patent Detective
description: Solve IP crime cases by investigating suspects and examining evidence
summary: Put on your detective hat and solve IP crimes! Investigate patent theft, trademark fraud, and infringement cases. Interview suspects, examine evidence, and crack the case!

cases.title: The Midnight Patent
cases.story:
A frantic call comes in at midnight. Dr. Sarah Chen, a robotics engineer, claims her revolutionary AI-powered prosthetic limb design has been stolen.

Three days ago, MegaTech Industries filed a patent for an identical invention. But Dr. Chen says she showed them her prototype 6 months ago during a partnership meeting.

MegaTech's CEO denies everything. Someone is lying.

Your mission: Uncover the truth.

suspects.name: Dr. Sarah Chen
suspects.statement:
I spent 3 years developing this technology in my garage lab. Last September, MegaTech invited me to discuss a partnership. I signed an NDA and showed them everything - my prototypes, my code, my neural interface design.

Two weeks later, they ghosted me. No calls returned. Then I see THEIR patent filing with MY exact design! They stole it!

suspects.name: James Park
suspects.statement:
This is absurd. Our R&D team has been working on prosthetic technology for 5 years. Yes, we met with Dr. Chen, but her design was primitive compared to ours.

We were considering acquiring her company, but her tech wasn't compatible with our systems. Our patent is based on work our team started in 2019. We have lab notebooks to prove it.
keyClaims: Have documentation of their own development

suspects.name: Dr. Lisa Wong
suspects.statement:
I've led the prosthetics team for 4 years. After the meeting with Dr. Chen, James asked me to 'explore similar approaches.' I thought it was strange timing...

Our patent filing happened very quickly after that meeting. Usually our approval process takes months, but this was fast-tracked. I... I'm not comfortable with how this went down.
keyClaims: CEO asked to 'explore similar approaches' after Chen meeting

evidence.name: NDA Document
evidence.content:
Date: September 12, 2023
Parties: Dr. Sarah Chen & MegaTech Industries

'All disclosed information, including prototypes, designs, and technical specifications, shall remain confidential and proprietary to the disclosing party.'

Signed by:
✍️ Dr. Sarah Chen
✍️ James Park (CEO, MegaTech)

evidence.name: Lab Notebook
evidence.content:
Entries from 2021-2023 showing detailed sketches of neural interface design. All entries are dated and witnessed by colleagues at her university lab.

Key entry (March 2022): 'Breakthrough! Neural interface successfully reads motor cortex signals with 94% accuracy.'

evidence.name: Patent Application
evidence.content:
Filed: March 7, 2024
Inventor: Dr. Lisa Wong
Assignee: MegaTech Industries

The neural interface design is identical to Dr. Chen's sketches from her lab notebook. Filed 6 months after the meeting with Dr. Chen.

evidence.name: Prior Work Documents
evidence.content:
General prosthetics research from 2019-2022. Shows work on mechanical prosthetics and basic motor control.

NO mention of neural interface technology. The design approach is completely different from what was filed in the patent.

evidence.name: Email Chain
evidence.content:
From: James Park
To: Dr. Lisa Wong
Date: September 20, 2023

'Fast-track the neural interface project. Use the approach from last week's meeting. File patent ASAP. This could be huge for Q4.'

Sent 8 days after the meeting with Dr. Chen.

evidence.name: Meeting Log
evidence.content:
MegaTech Building Security Log
Date: September 12, 2023

Visitor: Dr. Sarah Chen
Time In: 2:00 PM
Time Out: 4:30 PM
Meeting Attendees: James Park, Dr. Lisa Wong, Legal Team
Notes: Visitor brought prototype case (logged by security)

deductions.question: Who developed the neural interface technology first?
deductions.explanation: Dr. Chen's lab notebook shows development from 2021-2023, while MegaTech's prior work shows no neural interface research.

deductions.question: What proves MegaTech saw Dr. Chen's design?
deductions.explanation: The NDA document and meeting log confirm MegaTech saw Chen's prototype during the September 12 meeting.

deductions.question: What proves MegaTech copied the design?
deductions.explanation: James Park's email ordering the team to 'use the approach from last week's meeting' proves they copied Chen's design.

deductions.question: Did MegaTech have this technology before meeting Chen?
deductions.explanation: MegaTech's prior work documents show no neural interface technology before the meeting with Dr. Chen.

verdictOptions.text: Dr. Chen is lying - MegaTech developed it independently
MegaTech stole the invention after the NDA meeting
Both parties developed similar technology coincidentally
Dr. Wong acted alone without company knowledge

solution.explanation:
After Dr. Sarah Chen showed her neural interface design to MegaTech under NDA, CEO James Park saw an opportunity. Instead of partnering with her, he instructed his team to replicate her design and file a patent first.

The email evidence proves James Park ordered the fast-tracked patent based on 'last week's meeting.' MegaTech's prior work showed no neural interface technology - they only started after seeing Dr. Chen's prototype.
legalOutcome: Dr. Chen's patent is VALID (true inventor)
Dr. Chen can sue for damages and theft of trade secrets
solution.ipLesson: NDAs protect confidential information, but document everything! Dr. Chen's dated lab notebooks proved she was the original inventor. Always keep detailed records of your invention process with dates and witnesses.

cases.title: The Copycat Logo
cases.story:
Maya's Organic Café has been serving the community for 8 years with their distinctive green leaf logo. Last month, a new café called 'Maya's Natural Foods' opened across the street.

Their logo? Almost identical - same green leaf, similar font, same color scheme. Customers are confused, and Maya's business is suffering.

The new café owner claims it's just a coincidence. But Maya suspects trademark infringement.

Your mission: Determine if this is trademark fraud.

suspects.name: Maya Rodriguez
suspects.statement:
I opened Maya's Organic Café in 2016. I designed the logo myself - a green leaf with our name in a specific font. I registered the trademark in 2017.

Now this new place opens with almost the same logo! Customers keep coming to my café thinking we're the same business. Some even complain about the other café's service to me! This is hurting my reputation and sales.

suspects.name: David Chen
suspects.statement:
I just opened Maya's Natural Foods last month. My daughter's name is Maya, so I named it after her. The leaf logo represents natural, organic food - it's a common symbol!

I had no idea about the other café until after I opened. It's just a coincidence. Besides, my café focuses on takeout while hers is dine-in. We're different businesses.
keyClaims: Named café after his daughter Maya
Claims leaf logo is common symbol
Says he didn't know about original café
Claims businesses are different (takeout vs dine-in)

suspects.name: Jennifer Lee
suspects.statement:
David hired me to design his café logo in January. He specifically asked for a 'green leaf design with the name Maya's in a clean font.'

When I showed him initial concepts, he kept saying 'make it more like the successful organic café downtown.' I thought he meant the style, not copying someone specific. Now I realize he meant Maya's Organic Café...
keyClaims: David requested specific green leaf design
David said 'make it like the successful café downtown'
Designer now realizes David meant to copy

evidence.name: Original Trademark
evidence.content:
Trademark Registration
Registered: March 15, 2017
Owner: Maya Rodriguez
Mark: 'Maya's Organic Café' with green leaf design
Class: Restaurant services
Status: Active and in use

evidence.name: Logo Comparison
evidence.content:
Original (2017): Green leaf with 'Maya's Organic Café' in Montserrat font
New (2024): Green leaf with 'Maya's Natural Foods' in similar font

Similarities:
- Identical green color (#2ECC71)
- Same leaf shape and orientation
- Nearly identical font style
- Same layout (leaf above text)

evidence.name: Design Brief Email
evidence.description: Email from David to designer Jennifer
evidence.content:
From: David Chen
To: Jennifer Lee
Date: January 10, 2024

'Hi Jennifer, I need a logo for my new café. I want something like Maya's Organic Café downtown - they're really successful. Green leaf, clean font, professional look. Can you make something similar?'

evidence.name: Customer Complaints
evidence.description: Social media posts showing customer confusion
evidence.content:
Multiple social media posts:

'Went to Maya's today but the food was different? Did they change the menu?' - Posted at new location

'Maya's has a new location across town! Same logo!' - Incorrect assumption

'Why does Maya's have two locations with different menus?' - Confused customer

evidence.name: Location Map
evidence.content:
Both cafés are located on the same street, only 200 meters apart. They serve the same geographic market and customer base.

Both offer organic food and beverages. The services overlap significantly despite David's claim of being 'different businesses.'

evidence.name: Designer's Notes
evidence.content:
Design Revision Notes - January 2024

Revision 1: Client said 'leaf needs to be more like the downtown café'
Revision 2: Client said 'font should match the successful one'
Revision 3: Client said 'perfect, this is exactly what I wanted'

Note to self: Client seems to be copying existing café design.

deductions.question: Who has the legal trademark rights?
deductions.explanation: Maya Rodriguez registered her trademark in 2017, giving her exclusive rights to use the mark for restaurant services.

deductions.question: Is there likelihood of customer confusion?
deductions.explanation: Multiple social media posts show customers are confused between the two cafés, thinking they're the same business.

deductions.question: Did David intentionally copy the logo?
deductions.explanation: David's email explicitly asks the designer to make something 'like Maya's Organic Café downtown,' proving intentional copying.

deductions.question: Are the businesses in the same market?
deductions.explanation: Both cafés are on the same street serving the same geographic market with overlapping services (organic food and beverages).

verdictOptions.text: No infringement - it's just a coincidence
No infringement - businesses are different enough

solution.explanation:
David Chen deliberately copied Maya Rodriguez's registered trademark. The email evidence proves he specifically instructed his designer to create something 'like Maya's Organic Café downtown.'

The logos are nearly identical in color, design, and layout. Both businesses operate in the same geographic market selling similar products. Customer confusion is documented through social media posts.

David's claim of 'coincidence' is contradicted by his own email instructions to the designer.
legalOutcome: David's logo infringes Maya's registered trademark
David must cease using the infringing logo immediately
David must rebrand with a distinctly different logo
Maya can sue for damages and lost profits
David may face additional penalties for willful infringement
solution.ipLesson: Trademark law protects consumers from confusion and protects businesses from unfair competition. When marks are confusingly similar and used in the same market, it's infringement. Always conduct a trademark search before choosing a business name and logo. Intentional copying can result in higher damages.

cases.title: The Vanishing Algorithm
cases.story:
NeuraSoft Inc. has developed a breakthrough compression algorithm capable of reducing file sizes by 70% with zero quality loss.

Last week, a competitor called HyperZip suddenly launched a product using the same technique — down to identical variable names in the code.

NeuraSoft believes someone leaked their source code.

Your mission: Uncover how the trade secret was stolen.

suspects.name: Evan Brooks
suspects.statement:
I've worked at NeuraSoft for 5 years. I would never leak our code. Yes, I took my laptop home that weekend, but only because of deadlines.

Someone else must have accessed the repository. Maybe a break-in or a hack?

suspects.name: Marina Flores
suspects.statement:
I left NeuraSoft months before the final algorithm was finished. I never had access to the complete codebase.

HyperZip did contact me about a job, but I declined. I didn't share anything — I swear.
keyClaims: Claims no access to final algorithm

suspects.name: Leo Carter
suspects.statement:
HyperZip's tech is entirely our own. Compression research is competitive — similar solutions arise.

Any resemblance is purely coincidental.

evidence.name: Git Access Log
evidence.description: Repository access log showing unusual activity
evidence.content:
Access Log - October 14, 2024

User: EvanBrooks
Access Time: 2:13 AM
Action: Full repository download
Location: Unknown IP (London, UK)

Note: Evan was in California at the time.

evidence.name: Email From HyperZip
evidence.description: Recruitment email sent to former intern Marina
evidence.content:
From: careers@hyperzip.com
To: marina.flores

'We are particularly interested in candidates with experience on NeuraSoft's FileShrink algorithms. Any insights into their approach would be extremely valuable.'

evidence.name: Source Code Comparison
evidence.description: Side-by-side comparison of NeuraSoft and HyperZip code
evidence.content:
Identical variable names detected:
- bufferOptimizeLevel
- c_losslessFlag
- deltaMapThreshold

Algorithm structure is 95% identical.

evidence.name: Security Report
evidence.content:
October 14, 2024: Suspicious login detected under EvanBrooks account.

IP traced to HyperZip corporate office in London.

evidence.name: Laptop Metadata
evidence.content:
No signs of code copying or external device usage.

Activity logs confirm Evan was asleep during the unauthorized access.

evidence.name: Internal Chat Leak
evidence.description: HyperZip internal chat obtained by anonymous whistleblower
evidence.content:
CTO Leo Carter: 'We got the full repo — integrate everything before they notice.'
Timestamp: October 15, 2024

deductions.question: Who accessed the code repository?
deductions.explanation: The security report shows the login came from HyperZip's office, not Evan.

deductions.question: Did HyperZip obtain NeuraSoft's code illegally?
deductions.explanation: The code comparison shows 95% similarity, proving copying.

deductions.question: Was Evan responsible for the leak?
deductions.explanation: Forensic analysis proves Evan's laptop was not used.

deductions.question: Did HyperZip knowingly use stolen data?
deductions.explanation: The internal chat reveals they knowingly integrated stolen code.

verdictOptions.text: HyperZip hacked NeuraSoft and stole the code
Both companies coincidentally made similar algorithms

solution.verdict: HyperZip hacked NeuraSoft and stole the code
solution.explanation:
Evidence shows HyperZip used Evan's credentials to illegally access NeuraSoft's repository. The IP address matches HyperZip's office, and internal chats confirm they intentionally integrated the stolen code.

Evan was framed, and Marina had no access to the final algorithm.
legalOutcome: HyperZip faces criminal charges for cyber intrusion
HyperZip must cease product sales using stolen code
solution.ipLesson: Trade secrets require strong digital protection. Access logs, IP tracking, and forensic analysis can expose digital theft even when hackers use stolen credentials.

cases.title: The Stolen Fashion Sketchbook
cases.story:
A young designer claims her fashion sketches were stolen and used by a major clothing brand. Last month, the brand released a new clothing line identical to drawings from her sketchbook.

Your job is to find out who copied whom.

suspects.name: Lila Harper
suspects.statement:
I posted a few sketch previews online, but never the full designs. I met with TrendLine's recruiter in March and showed them my entire sketchbook.

Two weeks later, they stopped responding — and now the designs are on shelves!

suspects.name: Hannah Cole
suspects.statement: I meet dozens of designers every month. Yes, Lila showed me her sketches, but we decided not to move forward. Our new clothing line was already in development.
keyClaims: Claims designs were already in development

suspects.name: Mark Rivers
suspects.statement: I've never seen Lila's sketches. All our concepts were original and created within the team. Fashion trends overlap — similarities happen.
keyClaims: Claims no knowledge of Lila's work

evidence.name: Sketchbook Photos
evidence.content:
Sketchbook contains timestamped designs from January–March 2024.

Key sketches are identical to TrendLine's product line.

evidence.name: Product Catalog
evidence.content: Side-by-side comparison shows identical shapes, patterns, and stitching lines.

evidence.name: Recruitment Meeting Log
evidence.description: Log of Lila’s meeting with TrendLine
evidence.content:
Meeting Date: March 8, 2024
Attendees: Lila Harper, Hannah Cole
Notes: Lila presented full sketchbook for review.

evidence.name: Design Team Timeline
evidence.content:
Summer 2024 designs started April 2024 — one month after the meeting.

No earlier drafts exist.

deductions.question: Who created the designs first?
deductions.explanation: The dated sketchbook clearly predates TrendLine’s collection.

deductions.question: Did TrendLine see the original designs?
deductions.explanation: Meeting logs confirm they reviewed Lila’s full sketchbook.

deductions.question: Did TrendLine already have designs before meeting?
deductions.explanation: Their design process started after the meeting, proving copying.

verdictOptions.text: Both designers coincidentally created similar work

solution.explanation: TrendLine's internal timeline proves they only started designing after seeing Lila’s work. The similarities are too exact to be coincidence.
legalOutcome: TrendLine must pull products from sale
solution.ipLesson: Always date your creative work. Timestamped originals are strong copyright evidence.

cases.title: The Silent Microchip
cases.story: A startup claims a large electronics company copied its patented noise-canceling microchip. The big corporation denies it, saying they developed their own version independently.

suspects.name: Jacob Lin
suspects.statement:
We patented our design in 2021. Our chip uses a dual-wave cancellation method that no one else uses.

I showed it to MegaSound during partnership talks. A year later, they released an identical chip.

suspects.name: Rebecca Shah
suspects.statement: Our chip is completely different. We've been researching noise reduction since 2018. Any similarities reflect industry standards.

suspects.name: Alan Pierce
suspects.statement: Yes, we met Jacob, but only for business evaluation. We never accessed his schematics. It’s unfair to accuse us without proof.

evidence.name: Patent Diagram
evidence.content: Shows dual-wave cancellation nodes uniquely arranged in a triangular formation.

evidence.name: MegaSound Chip Analysis
evidence.content: Internal structure matches the triangular node design from Jacob’s patent.

evidence.name: Meeting Transcript
evidence.content: Transcript shows MegaSound reviewed the microchip diagrams.

evidence.name: MegaSound R&D History
evidence.content: MegaSound focused on acoustic hardware, not microchips. No record of noise-canceling tech pre-2022.

deductions.question: Which design came first?
deductions.explanation: Jacob’s 2021 patent predates MegaSound’s chip.

deductions.question: Did MegaSound have access to the design?
deductions.explanation: The transcript proves MegaSound reviewed the schematics.

deductions.question: Does MegaSound’s chip copy patented features?
deductions.explanation: Teardown reveals identical structures.

solution.explanation: MegaSound gained access to Jacob’s schematics during partnership talks, and their chip matches his patented structure exactly.
solution.ipLesson: Never share schematics without proper legal protections.

cases.title: The Counterfeit Sneakers
cases.story: A luxury shoe brand discovers counterfeit versions of its new sneaker model being sold online. The knockoffs are nearly identical, raising suspicion of an internal leak.

suspects.name: Adrian Lowe
suspects.statement: I oversee shipments but have no access to design files. Anyone blaming me is guessing.

suspects.name: Sasha Kim
suspects.statement: I worked on the sneaker, but my drafts weren’t finalized. I did take some sketches home, but only to study them.

suspects.name: Carlos Diaz
suspects.statement: I buy sneakers from a supplier in another country. I didn’t know they were counterfeit. They looked real to me!

evidence.name: Official Design Blueprint
evidence.content: Shows a hidden triangular stitch only visible on close inspection.

evidence.name: Counterfeit Shoe Photos
evidence.content: Counterfeit shoes contain the same hidden triangular stitch — a detail not shown in public teasers.

evidence.name: Sasha's Home Folder
evidence.description: Company audit discovered copied sketches on Sasha’s home laptop
evidence.content: Sketches include the hidden stitch pattern.

evidence.name: Supplier Invoice
evidence.content: Supplier specializes in counterfeit goods. Multiple prior investigations.

deductions.question: Did the counterfeiters have access to the hidden stitch design?
deductions.explanation: Counterfeit shoes used a non-public design element.

deductions.question: Who took design files outside the company?
deductions.explanation: Sasha had complete sketches on her personal laptop.

deductions.question: Did Carlos knowingly sell counterfeits?
deductions.explanation: His supplier is a known counterfeit source.

verdictOptions.text: Sasha leaked the designs leading to counterfeits

solution.explanation: Sasha took complete sketches home and those included non-public details, enabling counterfeiters to create near-perfect replicas.
solution.ipLesson: Even small design leaks can enable counterfeits. Protect proprietary sketches.

cases.title: The Duplicate App
cases.story: A small developer finds an app identical to his on the app store—same UI, same features, even the same bugs. He suspects the code was stolen.

suspects.name: Oliver Reed
suspects.statement:
I built my productivity app alone over two years. Suddenly, another app appears with the same animations and even the same rare crash.

This can’t be coincidence.

suspects.name: Nora Patel
suspects.statement: I helped Oliver briefly with UI advice, but I never touched his code. I work for various clients — but none involved copying.

suspects.name: ByteWorks LLC
suspects.statement: We created our app from scratch. Productivity apps often share similar layouts. We reject the allegation entirely.

evidence.name: GitHub Commit History
evidence.content: Shows two years of commits with original code development.

evidence.name: Binary Code Comparison
evidence.content:
ByteWorks app contains multiple identical function names with same typos.

Example: 'calulateProductivity()'

evidence.name: Error Log
evidence.description: Both apps show the same rare crash bug
evidence.content:
Bug triggered by opening settings rapidly.

Bug matches line-for-line in logs.

evidence.name: Consulting Contract
evidence.content: Specifically states she only provided UI mockup consultation.

deductions.question: Were the apps independently created?
deductions.explanation: Identical function names and typos show code copying.

deductions.question: Did Nora have access to core code?
deductions.explanation: Her contract limits her to UI mockups only.

deductions.question: Are the apps identical beyond UI?
deductions.explanation: Identical rare bug proves shared code source.

verdictOptions.text: Nora copied files for a client

solution.explanation: ByteWorks' app contains identical typos and bugs, which is impossible without copying. Nora had no access beyond UI advice.
legalOutcome: App may be removed from stores
solution.ipLesson: Unique errors and typos can be powerful evidence of software copying.

cases.title: The Miracle Supplement
cases.story: A wellness company claims that a rival brand is using a confusingly similar name and packaging for their new supplement — creating mass customer confusion.

suspects.name: Alicia Voss
suspects.statement:
We’ve been selling VitalPure since 2019. Now this new company launches 'VitaPure' with nearly identical bottles.

Customers think it’s us.

suspects.name: Greg Dalton
suspects.statement: Our name is different. Health brands use similar words. Our packaging uses a green leaf because it's natural. That’s normal.

suspects.name: Clara Mills
suspects.statement: Greg asked me to make packaging that looked like 'that successful health bottle.' I thought he meant general styles, not a specific brand!

evidence.name: Original Trademark Papers
evidence.content:
VitalPure™ — registered trademark for vitamin supplements.
Status: Active.

evidence.name: Packaging Comparison
evidence.content:
Both bottles:
- White matte finish
- Green leaf logo in upper corner
- Blue stripe border
- Nearly identical font

evidence.name: Internal Marketing Email
evidence.content: Greg: 'Make it resemble VitalPure — customers trust that brand. But change just enough to avoid legal issues.'

evidence.name: Customer Survey
evidence.content: 38% of customers believed VitaPure was a VitalPure sub-brand.

deductions.question: Does VitalPure have trademark protection?
deductions.explanation: VitalPure's trademark is active since 2020.

deductions.question: Is packaging confusingly similar?
deductions.explanation: Near-identical packaging creates confusion.

deductions.question: Was copying intentional?
deductions.explanation: Email explicitly states intent to resemble VitalPure.

verdictOptions.text: No infringement — they look different enough

solution.explanation: Greg’s email confirms intent to mimic the brand. Combined with high customer confusion, this is classic trademark infringement.
solution.ipLesson: Intentional copying leads to severe penalties in trademark law.

cases.title: The Ghost Inventor
cases.story: Two engineers claim to be the true inventor of a new solar coating technology. Only one name can legally appear on the patent.

suspects.name: Dr. Felix Stone
suspects.statement: I led the development. I created the polymer mixture formula myself. The whole idea began in my lab notebook.
keyClaims: Says idea came from his notebook

suspects.name: Nadine Hart
suspects.statement: Felix started it, sure. But I tweaked the formula to make it actually work. Without my adjustments, it was useless.

suspects.name: CEO Martin Hale
suspects.statement: From a business standpoint, naming Felix alone is simpler. He’s senior. But I don’t know the technical details.

evidence.name: Felix’s Lab Notebook
evidence.content:
Shows initial formula attempts from 2022.

Fails stability tests.

evidence.name: Nadine’s Experiment Log
evidence.content: February 2023 entry: Nadine adds stabilizing polymer, resulting in 300% efficiency increase.

evidence.name: Final Patent Draft
evidence.content: Final version of formula includes Nadine’s stabilizing agent.

evidence.name: Meeting Notes
evidence.content: CEO suggests only naming Felix to avoid 'complications.'

deductions.question: Who created the original concept?
deductions.explanation: Felix’s early formulas prove initial invention.

deductions.question: Whose work made the invention functional?
deductions.explanation: Nadine’s stabilizing agent is what enables the final working formula.

deductions.question: Which formula is used in the patent?
deductions.explanation: Final formula includes Nadine’s improvements.

verdictOptions.text: Both Felix and Nadine are co-inventors

solution.verdict: Both Felix and Nadine are co-inventors
solution.explanation: Felix devised the original concept, but Nadine’s contributions were essential to the final working invention. Patent law requires naming all inventors who contributed to the claims.
legalOutcome: Patent must list both as co-inventors
solution.ipLesson: Inventorship is about contribution to the claims — not job titles.

cases.title: The Missing Film Footage
cases.story: A documentary filmmaker discovers that another studio used her original drone footage in their film without permission.

suspects.name: Riley Moore
suspects.statement: I shot that drone footage myself. The sunrise angle, the mountain sweep — it's unmistakably mine. I never licensed it to anyone.

suspects.name: Derek Shaw
suspects.statement: We bought the footage legally from a freelancer. If Riley has an issue, she should talk to him — not us.

suspects.name: Freelancer 'SkyVids'
suspects.statement: I did shoot similar footage, but the file they used wasn’t mine. I only sold them one clip — maybe they mixed it up?

evidence.name: Original RAW File
evidence.content: Contains embedded metadata: Shot on July 4, 2023, GPS location embedded.

evidence.name: Studio Film Footage
evidence.content: Exact same angle, lighting, camera movement — pixel-perfect match.

evidence.name: Purchase Receipt
evidence.content: Shows studio purchased a different clip — not the one used.

evidence.name: SkyVids Portfolio
evidence.content: His footage differs significantly — different angle, lighting, and timestamps.

deductions.question: Is the footage identical?
deductions.explanation: Pixel-perfect match proves copying.

deductions.question: Did Riley shoot the original clip?
deductions.explanation: Metadata proves authorship.

deductions.question: Did the studio purchase the correct clip?
deductions.explanation: Receipt shows they bought a different clip entirely.

verdictOptions.text: Studio is innocent — they bought the exact footage used
Studio used Riley’s footage without permission

solution.verdict: Studio used Riley’s footage without permission
solution.explanation: The studio bought the wrong footage and ended up using Riley’s clip instead, violating copyright law.
legalOutcome: Film may require edits or takedown
solution.ipLesson: Always verify license rights before using creative content.
